History & Physical (Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
- 48-year-old man with 3-day history of watery, non-bloody diarrhoea (5–6×/day) that began after two episodes of vomiting, clinically assessed by telemedicine as probable acute viral gastroenteritis with mild dehydration; advised oral rehydration, symptomatic care, time off work, and follow-up if no improvement.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Acute onset diarrhoea.
  • Watery, loose stools, 5–6 bowel motions per day.  
  • Onset: 3 days ago; began with nausea and 2 episodes of vomiting. Vomiting has resolved.  
  • No visible blood or mucus.  
  • No abdominal pain or cramping reported.  
  • Subjective low-grade fever only on first day; currently afebrile.  
  • Feels “very weak” and dehydrated; poor oral intake; minimal appetite.  
- Exacerbating / relieving factors: None identified; no clear food trigger, no sick contacts known.  
- Associated / systems review (pertinent positives & negatives):  
  • (-) Headache, (-) myalgias, (-) urinary symptoms, (-) respiratory symptoms, (-) weight loss.  
  • (-) Recent antibiotic use, (-) recent travel, (-) hospital exposure.  

Past Medical History:
- Asthma, mild intermittent; uses salbutamol meter-dose inhaler (blue) PRN; no recent exacerbations.
- No other chronic illnesses mentioned.

Medications:
- Salbutamol inhaler PRN (dose/route/frequency not documented).

Allergies:
- No known drug allergies (NKDA).

Social History:
- Lives alone.  
- Occupation: Software engineer; currently off work for 3 days due to illness.  
- Tobacco: Never smoker.  
- Alcohol: Infrequent, social use.  
- Recreational drugs: Not mentioned.  

Family History:
- Father: Hypertension; died of bowel (colorectal) cancer ~10 years ago.  
- Mother: Type 2 diabetes mellitus.  
- No other heritable conditions noted.

Physical Examination:
- Telehealth visit; no vitals or physical findings recorded.

Investigations:
- None performed at this visit.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: Acute infectious gastroenteritis, likely viral
  • Assessment: Classic presentation of self-limited viral gastroenteritis (abrupt onset vomiting followed by watery diarrhoea, mild/short fever, no blood, no severe pain). Bacterial aetiology less likely; low suspicion for C. difficile or inflammatory bowel disease at this stage.  
  • Plan:  
    – Encourage high oral fluid intake (water, clear soups).  
    – Oral rehydration salts (e.g., Dioralyte) as directed by pharmacy.  
    – Gradual return to light diet as tolerated (BRAT or similar).  
    – Paracetamol for fever or malaise (dose not specified).  
    – Remain off work until diarrhoea-free for 24–48 h.  
    – Red-flag advice: seek care urgently for persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, blood in stool, high fever, severe abdominal pain, or signs of worsening dehydration.  
    – Follow-up: Re-assess if not improving within 5–7 days.

Issue 2: Mild dehydration
  • Assessment: Reports weakness, difficulty maintaining hydration; no objective vitals available.  
  • Plan: Same as above; monitor urine output; consider in-person review or emergency evaluation if dizziness, orthostatic symptoms, or reduced urine occur.

Issue 3: Asthma (background, stable)
  • Assessment: Well-controlled, uses salbutamol PRN only.  
  • Plan: Continue current inhaler as needed; no change.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Viral gastroenteritis (High) – abrupt onset vomiting → watery diarrhoea, short course, self-resolving pattern, absence of alarming features.
2. Bacterial food-borne gastroenteritis (Moderate) – time-frame compatible; lacks abdominal cramps, fever, or known food exposure but still possible.
3. Clostridioides difficile infection (Low) – watery diarrhoea possible but no recent antibiotics or healthcare exposure; low clinical suspicion.

Quality checks:
● Missing / expected elements: No vital signs, no physical examination, no formal medication reconciliation beyond inhaler, immunisation and travel history not explored, stool frequency documentation adequate but stool volume not quantified.  
● Conflicts: None between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Clear audio; minimal background noise; all key clinical details intelligible.
